categories.analogy: Like a keycard for a building: it works as long as you have it and someone didn't copy it, but there's no handshake verifying the building is the real one.
categories.description: The client includes a static or rotating secret key in each request header. The server looks up the key to authorize access. No certificates, no handshakes, no PKI.
categories.details: API keys are a shared secret between client and server, typically passed as X-API-Key or Authorization: ApiKey header. They're trivial to integrate: generate a key, distribute it out-of-band, and check it on the server side. Rotation is manual or assisted through a dashboard. The simplicity comes with trade-offs: keys are usually sent over TLS but not cryptographically bound to the connection, they're harder to revoke instantly at scale, and they provide no mutual authentication — only the client proves identity, never the server. Still, for many internal tooling and partner integrations, the operational savings are worth the security gap.
inScope: Third-party integrations where partners can't manage certificates
Internal tooling and CI/CD pipelines with low-security requirements
Public APIs where simplicity drives adoption and TLS provides transport security
outOfScope: High-value service meshes where key exfiltration risks are unacceptable
Regulated industries mandating cryptographic identity proofs
categories.primaryFocus: Minimal-friction integration for third-party and partner access
categories.subtitle: Shared secret in a header — the simplest way to identify a caller
categories.title: Simple API Key Authentication

categories.analogy: Like a signed conference badge: once issued and validated at the door, each session attendee checks the badge's hologram stamp instead of calling registration.
categories.description: A JSON Web Token carries signed claims about the caller's identity and permissions. The server validates the signature on every request without needing a session store or callback.
categories.details: JWTs are typically obtained via an initial auth flow (OAuth2, login endpoint) and then presented in the Authorization header. The issuer signs tokens with a private key; verifiers check with the corresponding public key. This eliminates per-request round-trips to an auth server and scales horizontally with ease. However, tokens have a finite lifetime — short-lived tokens mean frequent re-authentication, while long-lived tokens increase exposure if compromised. Revocation is also difficult since tokens are stateless by design.
inScope: Microservices that need fast per-request auth without database lookups
Single-page applications and mobile clients with intermittent connectivity
Federated identity where a central IdP issues tokens for downstream consumers
outOfScope: Service-to-service auth where you can't centralize token issuance
Environments requiring real-time revocation (tokens remain valid until expiry)
Replacing network-layer encryption — JWTs should always ride on TLS, not plaintext
categories.primaryFocus: Lightweight, stateless authentication that scales to high-throughput APIs
categories.subtitle: Stateless bearer tokens with embedded claims and signatures
categories.title: JWT-Based Authentication

categories.analogy: Like both parties at a business meeting flashing government-issued IDs verified by the same authority before sharing any confidential information.
categories.description: Both client and server present X.509 certificates during the TLS handshake, providing strong mutual authentication rooted in a trusted Certificate Authority.
categories.details: Every service holds a private key and certificate signed by a CA the peer trusts. The TLS 1.3 handshake validates both sides before any application data flows. This gives you cryptographic assurance of identity — not just IP allowlists or shared secrets. The cost is operational: you must provision, rotate, revoke, and store certificates across every service in the mesh.
inScope: Regulated environments requiring mutual verification (finance, healthcare, defense)
Scenarios where you control both client and server certificate lifecycle
outOfScope: Third-party integrations that can't manage X.509 certificates
Rapid prototyping where certificate overhead slows iteration
Public-facing consumer APIs where clients are browsers or mobile apps
categories.primaryFocus: Strong cryptographic identity for every endpoint
categories.subtitle: Mutual TLS — the gold standard for zero-trust service authentication
categories.title: Traditional mTLS with PKI

categories.analogy: Like a library card (OAuth2 token) that only works when presented alongside a government ID (client cert) — the card alone is insufficient.
categories.description: Extends standard OAuth2 flows by binding the client's TLS certificate to the token request, so access tokens are only valid when presented with the cert that requested them.
categories.details: RFC 8705 defines how to include a SANS_DNS or SANS_URI from the client certificate as a cnf (confirmation) claim in the issued token. The resource server then checks that the presenting client's certificate matches the bound claim. This gives you OAuth2's rich authorization framework — scopes, consent, token types — while anchoring the token to a specific mTLS identity. Integration is moderate: clients need certificate management, and resource servers must validate the cnf claim. The approach is ideal when third-party apps need OAuth2 scopes but you require stronger binding than a shared secret.
inScope: APIs offering OAuth2 scopes but requiring client cert binding for sensitive resources
Third-party partner integrations where you control authorization policies but not PKI
Replacing OAuth2 client_secret with cert-bound tokens for higher security
outOfScope: Simple internal services that don't need OAuth2's authorization granularity
Environments where clients cannot handle certificate-based TLS
Consumer-facing apps where certificate provisioning is a UX barrier
categories.primaryFocus: Strong authorization with cryptographic client binding for third-party integrations
categories.subtitle: Combining OAuth2 authorization with mTLS client binding
categories.title: OAuth2 with Client Certificates

categories.analogy: Like a secure relay station between every building in a campus — packages go through a guarded checkpoint that verifies sender and receiver, and the couriers inside each building never see the process.
categories.description: A service mesh like Istio, Linkerd, or Consul Connect injects sidecar proxies that automatically establish mTLS between services, with a built-in CA and transparent certificate rotation.
categories.details: Each service gets a co-located proxy (Envoy, Linkerd, etc.) that terminates TLS for inbound and initiates TLS for outbound traffic. The mesh control plane acts as the CA, issuing short-lived certificates and distributing root trust bundles. Application code makes plain HTTP calls to localhost; the sidecar handles the cryptographic details. This delivers mTLS security with near-zero application changes. The costs are operational: sidecar memory/CPU overhead, mesh control plane complexity, and an additional network hop per request. For large Kubernetes deployments, the trade-off usually favors the mesh.
inScope: Large Kubernetes clusters with dozens to hundreds of services
Organizations standardizing on a service mesh for traffic management anyway
Teams that want mTLS security without cert management in application code
outOfScope: Small deployments where sidecar overhead dominates resource budgets
Bare-metal or VM environments lacking mesh deployment tooling
Third-party external clients that cannot route through your mesh
categories.primaryFocus: Transparent mTLS at scale without modifying application code
categories.subtitle: Sidecar proxies handle all TLS — your application stays oblivious
categories.title: Service Mesh Automated mTLS

categories.analogy: Like a passport office inside your data center: workloads show proof of who they are, the office prints an expiring visa on the spot, and everyone trusts that office.
categories.description: SPIFFE defines a standard identity format (SPIFFE ID) and SPIRE implements a trust domain that automatically mints, rotates, and distributes short-lived X.509 certificates to workloads.
categories.details: Instead of manually managing a PKI, you deploy a SPIRE Server that acts as a local CA. Agents on each node attest the workload (by socket, TLS, Kubernetes tokens, or AWS IAM roles), then issue a short-lived certificate. Services fetch their identity and trust bundle through the SPIFFE Workload API on a Unix socket. This removes the certificate lifecycle burden from application code while retaining mTLS-grade cryptographic guarantees. The trade-off is infrastructure complexity: you operate SPIRE servers, agents, and node-level attestation pipelines.
inScope: Kubernetes clusters with frequent pod churn and ephemeral workloads
Organizations wanting mTLS security without baking PKI into each app
Multi-service environments needing a unified trust domain
outOfScope: Simple two-service integrations where deploying SPIRE is overkill
Edge devices or IoT where agent footprint and attestation complexity is prohibitive
Third-party SaaS clients that cannot run a SPIRE agent
categories.primaryFocus: Zero-touch certificate lifecycle in dynamic cloud-native environments
categories.subtitle: Automated certificate provisioning for cloud-native workloads
categories.title: SPIFFE/SPIRE Workload Identity
